doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Starting at Kentucky in 1973: students who could not play the literature
summary: In 1973 he found students needed remedial work, so he studied literature and built a syllabus, even making music ed students read scores.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well in 1973 when you sort of started out was this philosophy in place?

Well no, it was — first of all I learned that the students couldn’t play the pieces that I knew. That was the first thing I learned. Well some of them. You know there were three or four that were good students, really. And they played the kind of literature that I knew. And the next person would come in you know I’ve never heard him play before and they obviously needed remedial work to play a moderately difficult piece, not even a difficult one. Even less than medium. So I started to really study literature. Because you know when you go to conservatory your teacher hands you the Haydn Trumpet Concerto or they hand you some other piece, the Tomasi Concerto where — “Oh you can play piccolo trumpet? Oh you’re going to play the Brandenburg Concerto” because they might be able to. But see like I said, you don’t find the shortcomings by only exposing a small part of what that student knows. Because it’s like students, when I used to practice when I first went to Eastman I didn’t want to sound bad in a practice room. All I ever played were things that I felt like I could — you know I tried to get those things better. And I knew I couldn’t play below the staff worth a darn so I didn’t really do that too much because you know, so that’s what you try to learn by setting up a syllabus. Because it’s very expository. You know it shows what the student can’t do. So even though they’re using the same syllabus, later, when I developed it a few years down the road, when I had my first sabbatical that was the very first thing I did. Because I was sort of doing it but it was still a little on the hodge-podge side you know. I had music ed students, so I had to figure out a way to use the same syllabus for music ed students. Like I said, “Well we’re going
to transpose.” “Well I don’t need to transpose.” I said, “Okay here’s this score, tell me what note the French horn is playing in concert pitch.” “Oh. Oh let’s see, that’s a” I’m going —

That’s right. I’d say — the kids are way smarter than we are. I said, “If you can’t read the score they know it.” Because they know what their instruments can do and you don’t. Count lines you know. I said, “You can’t do that. You want to be an extraordinary band director. That means, it doesn’t mean you’re a genius. It means you’re out of the ordinary. There are no geniuses. There are extraordinary people. You know?
Okay I’m quoting — that’s quote number one today. I love it.
